domain: 2.3 TRAUMA, SHOCK, BURNS, NEUROTRAUMA & CRITICAL CARE (15 STATIONS)
topic: ABG in AKI — Hyperkalaemia & Metabolic Acidosis
stem: A 62-year-old post-operative man with acute kidney injury has the following arterial blood gas report: pH 7.10, PaO2 100 mmHg, PaCO2 30 mmHg (35–45), base excess -10 mmol/L (-2 to +2), and K+ 6.5 mmol/L. In view of these life-threatening abnormalities, which immediate intravenous agent should be administered first to protect the myocardium against fatal arrhythmias?
options: Soluble insulin 10 units with 50 mL of 50% dextrose
Sodium bicarbonate 8.4% slow intravenous infusion
10% calcium gluconate 10 mL over 3–5 minutes
Furosemide 80 mg intravenous bolus injection
Magnesium sulphate 2 g in 100 mL normal saline
optionRationales: Incorrect: IV insulin with 50% dextrose drives potassium intracellularly within 15–30 minutes, so it is given immediately after membrane stabilisation rather than first.
Incorrect: Sodium bicarbonate helps correct severe acidaemia and causes a modest intracellular K+ shift, but it does not acutely stabilise the cardiac resting membrane potential.
Correct: IV 10% calcium gluconate (10 mL over 3–5 minutes) acts within minutes to antagonise hyperkalaemia-induced myocardial excitability without lowering serum K+.
Incorrect: Loop diuretics promote renal potassium excretion only if the kidneys are responsive and act too slowly for emergent cardioprotection in oliguric AKI.
Incorrect: IV magnesium sulphate is indicated for torsades de pointes or eclampsia, not acute cardioprotection in hyperkalaemic metabolic acidosis.
clinicalPearl: Severe hyperkalaemia (K+ >= 6.5 mmol/L) with severe metabolic acidosis (pH 7.10, BE -10) is immediately life-threatening; always give IV 10% calcium gluconate first for membrane stabilisation before insulin-dextrose and nebulised salbutamol.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Assess pH (7.35–7.45), base excess (-2 to +2), and serum K+ together; severe acidaemia with hyperkalaemia mandates immediate myocardial membrane stabilisation.

domain: 2.3 TRAUMA, SHOCK, BURNS, NEUROTRAUMA & CRITICAL CARE (15 STATIONS)
stem: A 58-year-old man is admitted to the emergency trauma unit after sustaining an accidental head impact. An axial non-contrast CT brain slice is shown. Which pairing accurately identifies the primary abnormality and the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score at or below which endotracheal intubation is indicated?
options: Right basal ganglia intracerebral haemorrhage; GCS <= 8
Right extradural haematoma; GCS <= 10
Left basal ganglia ischaemic infarct; GCS <= 9
Right chronic subdural haematoma; GCS <= 12
Bilateral subarachnoid haemorrhage; GCS <= 11
optionRationales: Correct: The CT demonstrates a hyperdense parenchymal clot centred in the right basal ganglia with mild ventricular effacement, and a GCS <= 8 ('less than 8, intubate') mandates airway protection.
Incorrect: An extradural haematoma is an extra-axial biconvex lens-shaped collection bounded by cranial sutures rather than deep parenchymal hyperdensity, and intubation is triggered at GCS <= 8.
Incorrect: The hyperdense acute lesion is located in the right hemisphere by radiological convention and represents haemorrhage rather than a hypodense ischaemic infarct.
Incorrect: A chronic subdural haematoma appears as an extra-axial hypodense/isodense crescentic collection over the cerebral convexity, not a deep parenchymal bleed.
Incorrect: Subarachnoid haemorrhage tracks as hyperdensity within basal cisterns and cortical sulci rather than forming a focal right lentiform mass, and the intubation threshold is GCS <= 8.
clinicalPearl: Deep hyperdense intraparenchymal clot in the lentiform/basal ganglia region indicates intracerebral haemorrhage; monitor GCS across Eye (1–4), Verbal (1–5), and Motor (1–6) domains and intubate promptly at GCS <= 8.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Severe head injury is defined as GCS <= 8 (coma range 3–8), which is the standard threshold for definitive endotracheal intubation.

domain: 2.3 TRAUMA, SHOCK, BURNS, NEUROTRAUMA & CRITICAL CARE (15 STATIONS)
stem: A 25-year-old man presents with neck pain following a high-speed road traffic collision. Anteroposterior and lateral cervical spine radiographs are shown. Which bony injury is demonstrated on these films?
options: Type II odontoid peg fracture at C2
Bilateral C1 ring (Jefferson) burst fracture
Atlanto-occipital dissociation with soft-tissue swelling
Flexion teardrop fracture of the C7 vertebral body
Unilateral interfacetal dislocation at C4–C5
optionRationales: Incorrect: The C2 odontoid process is intact on these views, whereas the focal malalignment lies lower in the mid-cervical spine.
Incorrect: A Jefferson burst fracture involves lateral mass displacement of C1 best seen on an open-mouth odontoid view, not mid-cervical subluxation.
Incorrect: Atlanto-occipital dissociation disrupts the craniocervical junction above C1 rather than the C4–C5 facet joints.
Incorrect: There is no anteroinferior triangular bone fragment avulsed from C7; the anterior displacement and widened interspinous space sit at C4–C5.

Correct: The lateral radiograph shows anterior translation of C4 on C5 with facet joint locking/hyperflexion and widened interspinous space, while the AP view shows spinous process malalignment typical of C4–C5 unilateral interfacetal dislocation.
clinicalPearl: In cervical trauma X-rays, assess all four alignment lines (anterior vertebral, posterior vertebral, spinolaminar, and spinous tips) and examine clinically for midline tenderness and neurological deficits using NEXUS/Canadian C-spine rules.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Suspected cervical spine injury requires immediate triple immobilisation (manual in-line stabilisation, hard collar, and sandbags) before and during radiographic clearance.

domain: 2.3 TRAUMA, SHOCK, BURNS, NEUROTRAUMA & CRITICAL CARE (15 STATIONS)
topic: Hypovolaemic Shock & Fluid Deficit in Acute Diarrhoea
stem: A 40-year-old previously healthy man presents with confusion and restlessness after 2 days of profuse watery diarrhoea. On admission his BP is 80/40 mmHg, urine output is 5 mL/hr, and estimated total body water is 40 L. After establishing wide-bore intravenous access, what is the most appropriate immediate fluid and electrolyte management?
options: Slow 5% dextrose infusion at 100 mL/hr with immediate IV potassium chloride
Rapid IV 0.9% saline or Hartmann's bolus, delaying IV K+ until UOP > 0.5 mL/kg/hr
Immediate oral rehydration solution via nasogastric tube before starting IV fluids
Continuous 10% human albumin infusion over 6 hours while restricting crystalloids
IV sodium bicarbonate bolus combined with furosemide to stimulate urine output
optionRationales: Incorrect: 5% dextrose distributes across total body water rather than restoring intravascular volume in shock, and giving IV potassium during oliguria (5 mL/hr) risks fatal hyperkalaemia.

Correct: Severe hypovolaemic shock (~10% body weight deficit, ~6.7 L for a ~67 kg adult with 40 L TBW; losses of Na+, K+, Cl-, and HCO3-) requires immediate rapid IV isotonic crystalloid resuscitation, deferring K+ replacement until adequate urine output (> 0.5 mL/kg/hr) is restored.
Incorrect: Altered sensorium and profound hypotension (80/40 mmHg) contraindicate oral/enteral rehydration as primary resuscitation due to poor splanchnic perfusion and aspiration risk.
Incorrect: Albumin is neither first-line nor superior to balanced/isotonic crystalloids for diarrhoeal hypovolaemic shock, and crystalloid restriction worsens organ hypoperfusion.
Incorrect: Loop diuretics worsen intravascular volume depletion in pre-renal oliguria and must not be given in hypovolaemic shock.
clinicalPearl: In severe dehydration with shock, restore the intravascular compartment first with rapid isotonic crystalloid boluses (20 mL/kg), then replace the calculated deficit (10 mL/%/kg) and ongoing losses—never add IV K+ until urine output is established.

guideCitation.keyPoint: In severe surgical dehydration (altered sensorium, oliguria, impaired vitals), first restore intravascular volume with a 20 mL/kg IV crystalloid bolus over 30 minutes before replacing the remaining deficit.

sourceStation.title: Hypovolaemic Shock & Fluid Deficit in Acute Diarrhoea
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
19. 40-year-old previously well male presented with confusion and restlessness. He has a 2-day history of diarrhoea. On admission: BP 80/40 mmHg, Urine output 5 mL/hr, Total body water 40 L.
19.1 Calculate the fluid deficit.
19.2 What are the ions that are lost?
19.3 What is the treatment?  [Text-only clinical calculation station]
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (19.1) Fluid deficit: Severe dehydration (~10% body weight loss). Since TBW ≈ 60% BW, TBW 40 L corresponds to ~67 kg adult → 10% BW ≈ 6.7 L (or if estimated as 10% of TBW = 4.0 L; note both calculations clearly). (19.2) Ions lost: Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, and HCO₃⁻. (19.3) Treatment: Immediate rapid IV isotonic crystalloid resuscitation (0.9% NaCl or Hartmann's/Ringer's lactate) to restore BP & perfusion, followed by deficit + ongoing loss replacement and IV potassium supplementation once urine output is adequate (> 0.5 mL/kg/hr).

domain: 2.3 TRAUMA, SHOCK, BURNS, NEUROTRAUMA & CRITICAL CARE (15 STATIONS)
stem: A 75-year-old man presents with progressive confusion and altered behaviour 3 days after a fall at home. A non-contrast CT brain scan is shown. Which diagnosis and definitive surgical treatment pair best accounts for these appearances?
options: Acute extradural haematoma; urgent craniotomy and middle meningeal artery ligation
Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage; nimodipine and endovascular coiling
Acute territorial ischaemic stroke; intravenous alteplase thrombolysis
Subacute/chronic subdural haematoma; urgent neurosurgical burr-hole drainage
Hypertensive basal ganglia haemorrhage; osmotic therapy and blood pressure lowering
optionRationales: Incorrect: Extradural haematomas form biconvex (lentiform) hyperdense collections limited by cranial sutures rather than a crescent-shaped collection tracking along the hemisphere.
Incorrect: Subarachnoid haemorrhage fills basal cisterns and sulcal spaces with bright acute blood rather than producing a unilateral extra-axial crescentic mass.
Incorrect: An ischaemic stroke produces parenchymal hypoattenuation conforming to a vascular territory without an extra-axial fluid collection.

Correct: The CT reveals a crescent-shaped (concavo-convex) extra-axial collection crossing suture lines with sulcal/ventricular effacement and midline shift, characteristic of a subacute/chronic subdural haematoma managed definitively by burr-hole drainage (or craniotomy if solid acute clot).
Incorrect: Hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage appears as a focal hyperdense clot deep within the brain parenchyma rather than an extra-axial convexity collection.
clinicalPearl: Subdural haematomas arise from torn bridging cortical veins in elderly or anticoagulated patients, creating a crescentic collection crossing suture lines; liquid chronic/subacute clots are evacuated via burr-hole drainage.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Prompt GCS monitoring and non-contrast CT imaging distinguish extra-axial surgical emergencies requiring neurosurgical evacuation after traumatic falls in older adults.

sourceStation.title: Right Subacute/Chronic Subdural Haematoma (CT Brain)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
04. A 75-year-old male presented to NCTH Ragama with altered behaviour. He has a past history of a fall 3 days ago. A CT image is shown below.
1. List three abnormalities seen in the image.
2. What is the likely diagnosis?
3. What is the definitive management?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) Abnormalities: Right crescent-shaped (concavo-convex) extra-axial collection crossing suture lines (hyper/isodense subacute), effacement of right cortical sulci & lateral ventricle, and midline shift to the left. (2) Diagnosis: Right acute-on-chronic / subacute subdural haematoma (SDH). (3) Definitive management: Urgent neurosurgical Burr-hole drainage (for chronic/subacute liquid SDH) or craniotomy (if large acute solid clot).

domain: 2.3 TRAUMA, SHOCK, BURNS, NEUROTRAUMA & CRITICAL CARE (15 STATIONS)
stem: A 28-year-old motorcyclist develops severe dyspnoea, hypotension, and engorged neck veins after blunt chest trauma. A chest radiograph obtained in the resuscitation bay is shown. Which immediate life-saving intervention is indicated for this condition?
options: Immediate needle decompression (2nd ICS mid-clavicular) followed by chest drain
Urgent subxiphoid pericardiocentesis under bedside ultrasound guidance
Rapid sequence endotracheal intubation with high positive end-expiratory pressure
Intravenous furosemide bolus with high-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask
Supine positioning with aggressive IV colloid infusion and repeat radiograph
optionRationales: Correct: The radiograph shows a massive right tension pneumothorax (hyperlucent hemithorax without lung markings, collapsed right lung, depressed right hemidiaphragm, and leftward mediastinal shift), requiring immediate wide-bore needle decompression (2nd ICS mid-clavicular or 4th/5th ICS anterior axillary line) followed by intercostal chest tube insertion.
Incorrect: Pericardiocentesis treats cardiac tamponade rather than unilateral pleural air under pressure causing lung collapse and contralateral tracheal deviation.
Incorrect: Positive-pressure ventilation prior to pleural decompression rapidly worsens intrathoracic pressure and precipitates obstructive cardiac arrest.
Incorrect: Diuretics have no role in obstructive shock from pleural air entrapment and will exacerbate preload compromise.
Incorrect: Delaying decompression for fluid boluses or repeat films risks imminent cardiorespiratory arrest; clinically recognised tension pneumothorax should be decompressed even before X-ray.
clinicalPearl: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis (hypotension, hyperresonance, absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation); never delay needle decompression for a chest X-ray, and always follow with an underwater-seal ICD.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Tension pneumothorax shows absent lung markings, ipsilateral lung collapse, contralateral mediastinal shift, and hemidiaphragm depression—mandating immediate decompression.

sourceStation.title: Right-Sided Tension Pneumothorax & Immediate Management
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
1.1 What is the diagnosis?
1.2 What is the immediate management of this patient?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1.1) Right-sided tension pneumothorax. (1.2) Immediate management: Immediate needle decompression (wide-bore 14G–16G cannula into 2nd intercostal space mid-clavicular line or 4th/5th ICS anterior/mid-axillary line — do NOT delay for X-ray clinically!) followed immediately by Intercostal Drainage (ICD) tube insertion connected to an underwater seal.

domain: 2.3 TRAUMA, SHOCK, BURNS, NEUROTRAUMA & CRITICAL CARE (15 STATIONS)
stem: A 35-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Treatment Unit after a road traffic accident with massive haemoperitoneum. His pulse rate is 130 bpm with reduced pulse pressure, capillary refill time is 3 seconds, and respiratory rate is 33/min (reference table shown). After securing two wide-bore intravenous cannulae, what is the most appropriate initial fluid resuscitation strategy?
options: Slow maintenance 5% dextrose infusion at 100 mL/hr while awaiting cross-match
Restricted 500 mL normal saline over 4 hours until blood pressure normalises
Rapid 1–2 L warmed isotonic crystalloid bolus with early blood transfusion
Immediate 1 L bolus of 6% hydroxyethyl starch colloid without crystalloid
Hypertonic 3% saline 250 mL infusion followed by oral electrolyte replacement
optionRationales: Incorrect: Maintenance dextrose does not remain in the intravascular space and leaves Class III haemorrhagic shock (30–40% blood loss) critically under-resuscitated.
Incorrect: Giving only 500 mL over 4 hours fails to restore circulating volume in a patient with tachycardia 130 bpm, tachypnoea 33/min, and falling systolic BP.

Correct: Clinical parameters fit Class III haemorrhage (30–40% volume loss, ~1,500–2,000 mL), requiring immediate rapid infusion of 1–2 L warmed isotonic crystalloid (0.9% NaCl or Hartmann's/Ringer's lactate) over 15–30 minutes with early balanced blood transfusion and urgent surgical haemorrhage control.
Incorrect: Synthetic starch colloids are avoided in acute haemorrhagic shock due to coagulopathy and nephrotoxicity; isotonic crystalloids and blood products are standard.
Incorrect: Hypertonic saline with oral replacement is inappropriate for massive intraperitoneal haemorrhage requiring IV volume resuscitation and emergency laparotomy.
clinicalPearl: Class III haemorrhage (30–40% loss, ~1.5–2.0 L) marks the onset of measurable hypotension alongside PR > 120 bpm and RR 30–40/min; resuscitate via two wide-bore cannulae with warmed isotonic crystalloids and early blood products.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Grade III haemorrhagic shock corresponds to 30–40% blood loss (1,500–2,000 mL) with pulse 120–140 bpm, hypotension, tachypnoea, and oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/hr).

sourceStation.title: Class III Haemorrhagic Shock (RTA Haemoperitoneum)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
2. 35-year-old male patient admitted to the ETU due to an RTA with a massive haemorrhagic lesion in the peritoneum. His pulse rate is 130 bpm with reduced pulse pressure, capillary refilling time is 3 s with respiratory rate 33/min (ACS Acute Hemorrhage table shown).

2.2 Write down two isotonic crystalloids given to the patient.

(2.3) Fluid rate: Rapid IV bolus of 1–2 L (warmed crystalloid via two wide-bore cannulae over 15–30 minutes, reassessing haemodynamic response and transitioning early to blood/balanced transfusion + urgent laparotomy).

domain: 2.4 ORTHOPAEDICS & MUSCULOSKELETAL (4 STATIONS)
stem: An elderly woman presents with wrist pain and deformity following a fall onto an outstretched hand. Anteroposterior and lateral wrist radiographs are shown. Which bone fracture and displacement pattern are demonstrated?
options: Distal ulna fracture with volar angulation and ulnar shortening
Distal radius fracture with volar displacement and intact dorsal cortex
Scaphoid waist fracture with dorsal intercalated segment instability
Proximal radial shaft fracture with radial head subluxation
Distal radius fracture with dorsal displacement and radial shortening
optionRationales: Incorrect: The primary transverse metaphyseal break involves the distal radius rather than the distal ulna, although the radial and ulnar styloids now sit at the same level from radial collapse.
Incorrect: Volar displacement of the distal radius describes a Smith's or volar Barton's fracture, whereas the lateral film here shows posterior (dorsal) tilting.
Incorrect: The scaphoid waist contour is preserved; the obvious cortical disruption crosses the distal radial metaphysis.
Incorrect: Proximal radius fractures do not account for this extra-articular distal metaphyseal wrist deformity.

Correct: The radiographs show a transverse distal radial metaphyseal fracture with dorsal (posterior) displacement/angulation and radial shortening aligning the radial and ulnar styloids—typical of a Colles'-type fracture.
clinicalPearl: A Colles' fracture occurs within ~2.5 cm of the distal radial articular surface with dorsal displacement, dorsal angulation, radial deviation, and radial shortening ('dinner-fork' deformity).

guideCitation.keyPoint: Colles' fracture is a transverse distal radial fracture whose distal fragment is displaced and angulated posteriorly (dorsally), producing the classic dinner-fork deformity.

sourceStation.title: Distal Radius Fracture (Colles'-Type Displacement)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:

sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (A) Radius (distal radius). (B) Displacement: Fracture at the distal neck/metaphysis of radius with dorsal (upward/posterior) displacement and radial shortening, aligning radial and ulnar styloid processes at the same level on AP view (typical Colles'-type pattern).

domain: 2.4 ORTHOPAEDICS & MUSCULOSKELETAL (4 STATIONS)
stem: A 72-year-old woman is unable to stand or bear weight after a fall at home. An anteroposterior radiograph of the injured hip is shown. What is the exact anatomical site of the fracture?
options: Left superior pubic ramus
Left subtrochanteric femoral shaft
Left posterior acetabular wall
Left femoral neck (neck of femur)
Right intertrochanteric femur
optionRationales: Incorrect: The pelvic ring and superior pubic ramus remain continuous on this view.
Incorrect: The cortex below the lesser trochanter (subtrochanteric region) is intact.
Incorrect: The acetabular dome and margins are preserved around the femoral head.
Correct: There is cortical disruption across the left femoral neck with loss of Shenton's line continuity, diagnostic of an intracapsular left neck-of-femur fracture.
Incorrect: Both laterality (left hip shown) and anatomical zone (intracapsular femoral neck rather than intertrochanteric line) are inaccurate here.
clinicalPearl: Intracapsular femoral neck fractures disrupt the retinacular blood supply to the femoral head (risking avascular necrosis), typically requiring hemiarthroplasty or total hip replacement in elderly patients.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Confirm suspected fractures with AP/lateral radiographs and systematically inspect cortical continuity, alignment lines, and distal limb neurovascular status.

sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Left femoral neck (neck of femur) fracture.

domain: 2.4 ORTHOPAEDICS & MUSCULOSKELETAL (4 STATIONS)
stem: A patient presents with a painless, well-circumscribed swelling over the dorsomedial aspect of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. A bedside examination manoeuvre is performed as shown. What does this sign indicate, and which lesion typically produces it?
options: Solid vascular tissue; capillary haemangioma
Clear fluid-filled cavity; ganglion cyst
Caseous necrotic material; tuberculous cold abscess
Keratin-filled subcutaneous sac; epidermoid cyst
Purulent exudate; acute septic bursitis
optionRationales: Incorrect: Solid or blood-filled vascular lesions absorb light rather than allowing brilliant transmission across the swelling.

Correct: The glowing illumination demonstrates a positive transillumination test, signifying a cystic lesion containing clear serous/mucinous fluid such as a ganglion cyst (as well as hydrocele, cystic hygroma, or epididymal cyst).
Incorrect: Thick caseous material is opaque and fails to transilluminate brightly.
Incorrect: Epidermoid (sebaceous) cysts contain opaque cheesy keratin and are classically transillumination-negative.
Incorrect: Acute pus scatters and blocks light transmission, rendering septic collections opaque on transillumination.
clinicalPearl: A positive transillumination test indicates clear fluid inside a cystic swelling (e.g., ganglion cyst, vaginal hydrocele, epididymal cyst, cystic hygroma); blood, pus, keratin, and solid tumours do not transilluminate.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Bedside lump assessment combines inspection, palpation, fluctuation, and transillumination to distinguish clear-fluid cysts from solid or purulent swellings.

(3) Two lumps: Ganglion cyst (or synovial cyst / adventitial bursa over 1st MTP), Hydrocele (vaginal hydrocele), Cystic hygroma, Epididymal cyst.

domain: 2.4 ORTHOPAEDICS & MUSCULOSKELETAL (4 STATIONS)
stem: A 62-year-old man with chronic alcoholic liver disease presents with painless, progressive cord-like thickening in the palm and an inability to lay his hand flat on a tabletop, as shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Ulnar nerve claw hand
Trigger finger (stenosing tenosynovitis)
Volkmann's ischaemic contracture
Dupuytren's contracture
De Quervain's tenosynovitis
optionRationales: Incorrect: Ulnar claw hand results from intrinsic muscle paralysis producing MCP hyperextension and IP flexion without fibrotic palmar fascial cords.
Incorrect: Trigger finger causes painful catching or locking of a flexor tendon at the A1 pulley without visible longitudinal palmar fascial cords.
Incorrect: Volkmann's contracture follows forearm compartment ischaemia and involves deep flexor muscle fibrosis across the forearm and wrist.

Correct: Thickened fibrotic cords in the palmar aponeurosis pulling the ring/little finger into fixed MCP/PIP flexion—associated with cirrhosis, alcohol excess, diabetes, phenytoin, and family history—are classic for Dupuytren's contracture.
Incorrect: De Quervain's tenosynovitis causes radial wrist pain over the first extensor compartment (positive Finkelstein test) rather than palmar flexion cords.
clinicalPearl: Dupuytren's contracture affects the palmar fascia (most commonly the ring and little fingers) and is tested clinically with Hueston's tabletop test; key associations include alcohol excess, cirrhosis, diabetes, phenytoin, and manual vibration.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Distinguish fixed palmar fascial cords with MCP/PIP flexion (Dupuytren's contracture) from ulnar nerve palsy clawing (MCP hyperextension with IP flexion from lumbrical paralysis).

sourceStation.title: Dupuytren's Contracture
sourceStation.originalPrompt: 01. What is the diagnosis?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Dupuytren's contracture (fibromatosis/thickening and contracture of the palmar fascia/aponeurosis; associations: family history, alcohol excess, diabetes, phenytoin, cirrhosis).

domain: 2.5 VASCULAR, DIABETIC FOOT & SOFT-TISSUE INFECTIONS (12 STATIONS)
stem: A 68-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history presents with progressive black discoloration of his right first and second toes, as shown. Which clinical entity and most common underlying cause explain this appearance?
options: Dry gangrene; peripheral arterial disease (atherosclerosis)
Wet gangrene; polymicrobial necrotising soft-tissue sepsis
Erysipelas; acute Group A streptococcal dermal infection
Acute deep vein thrombosis; phlegmasia caerulea dolens
Chronic fungal paronychia; untreated tinea pedis
optionRationales: Correct: Shriveled, desiccated, mummified black digits with a sharp line of demarcation represent dry gangrene due to chronic arterial insufficiency—most commonly atherosclerosis (also diabetes mellitus or Buerger's disease).
Incorrect: Wet gangrene produces swollen, boggy, blistering, foul-smelling tissue with indistinct demarcation and spreading proximal cellulitis.
Incorrect: Erysipelas causes bright fiery-red, raised, sharply demarcated plaques without black mummified digital necrosis.
Incorrect: Phlegmasia caerulea dolens causes acute tense oedema and cyanosis of the entire limb rather than chronic desiccated auto-amputating toes.
Incorrect: Superficial fungal nail/skin infection does not cause full-thickness ischaemic digital necrosis.
clinicalPearl: Dry gangrene develops from gradual arterial occlusion leading to mummification and a clear line of demarcation; key causes are atherosclerosis, diabetes mellitus, and thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger's disease).

guideCitation.keyPoint: Evaluate any gangrenous digit for underlying vascular occlusion (atherosclerosis, diabetes, Buerger's), pedal pulses, and signs of superadded wet infection.

sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (A) Dry gangrene of the right great (1st) and 2nd toes. (B) Causes: Peripheral arterial disease (atherosclerosis), Diabetes mellitus (micro/macrovascular), Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger's disease), Arterial embolism/thrombosis, Severe Raynaud's/vasculitis.

domain: 2.5 VASCULAR, DIABETIC FOOT & SOFT-TISSUE INFECTIONS (12 STATIONS)
stem: A 45-year-old labourer develops agonising limb pain, tense swelling, bronze skin discoloration, and palpable subcutaneous crepitus 24 hours after a soil-contaminated thigh laceration. Gram stain of wound exudate demonstrates large Gram-positive bacilli with subterminal spores. Alongside urgent radical surgical debridement, which causative organism and intravenous antibiotic regimen are indicated?
options: Staphylococcus aureus; IV flucloxacillin plus vancomycin
Streptococcus pyogenes; IV amoxicillin plus gentamicin
Clostridium perfringens; high-dose IV benzylpenicillin plus clindamycin
Pseudomonas aeruginosa; IV ceftazidime plus ciprofloxacin
Bacteroides fragilis; IV metronidazole monotherapy
optionRationales: Incorrect: Staphylococcus aureus appears as Gram-positive cocci in clusters and does not form spores or classic clostridial myonecrosis with gas.
Incorrect: Streptococcus pyogenes forms Gram-positive cocci in chains rather than spore-bearing bacilli.

Correct: Gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis) is caused by Clostridium perfringens (anaerobic Gram-positive spore-forming bacilli) and requires radical debridement plus high-dose IV benzylpenicillin (Penicillin G) and clindamycin (which suppresses bacterial exotoxin synthesis).
Incorrect: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a Gram-negative aerobic rod rather than a Gram-positive spore-former.
Incorrect: Bacteroides fragilis is a non-spore-forming Gram-negative anaerobe, and metronidazole monotherapy is inferior to penicillin plus clindamycin for C. perfringens myonecrosis.
clinicalPearl: Clostridium perfringens causes rapidly fatal gas gangrene via alpha-toxin (lecithinase); combine immediate radical debridement with high-dose IV benzylpenicillin plus clindamycin (to halt toxin translation).

guideCitation.keyPoint: Benzylpenicillin (Penicillin G / Crystalline penicillin IV) plus anaerobic/clostridial cover (with clindamycin toxin suppression and radical surgical debridement) treats severe clostridial soft-tissue necrosis.

sourceStation.title: Gas Gangrene (Clostridium perfringens)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:

1.) What is the organism?
2.) Drug(s) used on him?  [Micrograph omitted in 2012 archive files]
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Organism: Clostridium perfringens (non-motile Gram-positive bacilli with subterminal spores; double zone of beta-haemolysis). Drugs: High-dose IV Benzylpenicillin (Penicillin G) + Clindamycin (inhibits toxin synthesis; Drive key also notes Metronidazole/Gentamicin for polymicrobial cover) alongside urgent radical surgical debridement.

domain: 2.5 VASCULAR, DIABETIC FOOT & SOFT-TISSUE INFECTIONS (12 STATIONS)
stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with acute fever, rigors, and a tender, bright erythematous plaque spreading up her lower leg, as shown. Which clinical diagnosis and most likely causative organism correspond to this presentation?
options: Necrotising fasciitis; Clostridium perfringens
Deep cellulitis; Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Erythrasma; Corynebacterium minutissimum
Venous stasis dermatitis; Staphylococcus epidermidis
Erysipelas; Streptococcus pyogenes
optionRationales: Incorrect: Necrotising fasciitis presents with pain out of proportion, haemorrhagic bullae, dusky necrosis, and systemic shock rather than a well-demarcated bright red superficial plaque.
Incorrect: Cellulitis has indistinct, poorly demarcated borders involving deeper subcutaneous fat, and Pseudomonas is uncommon in immunocompetent community lower-limb plaques.
Incorrect: Erythrasma causes chronic reddish-brown scaly intertriginous patches (axillae/groin) showing coral-red fluorescence under Wood's light.
Incorrect: Stasis dermatitis is a chronic non-infective eczematous process lacking acute fever, rigors, and a raised advancing border.

Correct: A raised, fiery-red, palpable plaque with a sharply demarcated advancing border is classic erysipelas (superficial dermal/lymphatic infection), most commonly caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus).
clinicalPearl: Unlike cellulitis (diffuse, poorly demarcated subcutaneous infection), erysipelas involves the upper dermis and lymphatics, giving a palpable, sharply demarcated edge caused primarily by Streptococcus pyogenes.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Erysipelas involves the superficial dermis and presents as a palpable erythematous lesion with a well-demarcated edge caused mainly by beta-haemolytic streptococci (Streptococcus pyogenes).

sourceStation.title: Erysipelas (Streptococcus pyogenes)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
02)
a) What is the diagnosis? (Picture shown)
b) Most likely organism for above diagnosis.
c) Name 3 antibiotics for above condition.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (a) Erysipelas. (b) Organism: Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus). (c) Antibiotics: IV Penicillin G (Benzylpenicillin) 1.2 MU 6-hourly, Oral/IV Amoxicillin, Cephalexin 500 mg TDS, or Erythromycin 500 mg QDS/BD (or Clindamycin) if penicillin-allergic.

domain: 2.5 VASCULAR, DIABETIC FOOT & SOFT-TISSUE INFECTIONS (12 STATIONS)
stem: A 52-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes presents with a 2-day history of fever, warmth, and diffuse swelling of his distal leg and ankle, as shown. Which organism is most frequently responsible, and which intravenous antibiotic is appropriate for initial ward management?
options: Pseudomonas aeruginosa; oral ciprofloxacin monotherapy
Streptococcus pyogenes; IV flucloxacillin or cefuroxime
Clostridium perfringens; IV metronidazole monotherapy
Escherichia coli; IV gentamicin plus oral trimethoprim
Corynebacterium minutissimum; topical miconazole cream
optionRationales: Incorrect: Pseudomonas is typically associated with puncture wounds through footwear or malignant otitis externa rather than routine community lower-limb cellulitis.

Correct: Diffuse, poorly demarcated erythema and oedema of the lower limb indicates cellulitis (deep dermal and subcutaneous tissue), caused predominantly by Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus and treated on the ward with IV flucloxacillin, co-amoxiclav, or cefuroxime.
Incorrect: Metronidazole covers strict anaerobes and lacks activity against beta-haemolytic streptococci and staphylococci.
Incorrect: Gentamicin lacks reliable streptococcal and staphylococcal cover for routine lower-limb cellulitis.
Incorrect: Corynebacterium minutissimum causes superficial erythrasma in skin folds rather than acute febrile lower-limb cellulitis.
clinicalPearl: Lower limb cellulitis spreads through subcutaneous planes with indistinct margins; cover both Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus empirically (e.g., IV flucloxacillin or co-amoxiclav, or vancomycin/clindamycin if severe/MRSA).

guideCitation.keyPoint: Ward treatment of acute lower-limb cellulitis targets Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus using IV penicillins (crystalline penicillin/cloxacillin or co-amoxiclav), or clindamycin in penicillin allergy.

sourceStation.title: Lower Limb Cellulitis
sourceStation.originalPrompt:

sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Condition: Cellulitis. Organism: Streptococcus pyogenes (and Staphylococcus aureus). Ward antibiotics: IV Flucloxacillin / Co-amoxiclav / Cefuroxime (Drive PPTX lists Vancomycin, Clindamycin for severe/MRSA cases).

domain: 2.5 VASCULAR, DIABETIC FOOT & SOFT-TISSUE INFECTIONS (12 STATIONS)
stem: A 63-year-old man with long-standing Type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with the deep ankle-region ulcer shown. After haemodynamic stabilisation, empirical IV antibiotics, and deep tissue sampling for culture, which local surgical intervention is most essential?
options: Primary closure of the wound edges with interrupted nylon sutures
Sharp surgical debridement of all slough and necrotic tissue
Immediate split-thickness skin grafting over the sloughy base
Application of tight graduated compression bandaging to the calf
Daily dry gauze packing without excision of devitalised tissue
optionRationales: Incorrect: Primary suturing of an infected, necrotic diabetic wound traps bacteria and pus, worsening deep space sepsis.

Correct: Infected diabetic foot ulcers contain devitalised slough and necrotic tissue that harbour organisms and prevent healing; thorough surgical debridement alongside broad-spectrum antibiotics, glycaemic control, vascular assessment, and offloading is essential.
Incorrect: Skin grafts fail when placed over infected or sloughy beds; healthy pink granulation tissue and infection clearance are prerequisites.
Incorrect: Tight compression is contraindicated in diabetic foot ulcers until arterial ischaemia is excluded and sepsis is controlled.
Incorrect: Leaving necrotic slough in situ sustains bacterial biofilms and delays wound contraction and epithelialisation.
clinicalPearl: Every diabetic foot ulcer requires probing for exposed bone (osteomyelitis), palpation/Doppler of pedal pulses, thorough surgical debridement of slough, deep tissue culture, glycaemic optimisation, and pressure offloading.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Optimise glycaemic control strictly in diabetic surgical patients and manage dirty/infected wounds with surgical debridement, deep culture-guided IV antibiotics, and delayed healing.

sourceStation.title: Infected Diabetic Foot Ulcer
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
3. This is a wound of a Type 2 DM patient.
1. List 2 features of the wound which help in further management.
2. List 3 steps taken to manage the wound.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) Wound features: Size/depth & probing to bone (osteomyelitis), presence of slough/necrotic tissue vs granulation tissue, purulent discharge/erythema/oedema (infection), and surrounding callus/vascularity. (2) Management steps: (a) Surgical debridement of slough/necrotic tissue & deep tissue culture; (b) Empirical broad-spectrum IV/oral antibiotics + strict glycaemic control; (c) Vascular assessment (Doppler/ABI), offloading pressure, and moist sterile dressings.

domain: 2.5 VASCULAR, DIABETIC FOOT & SOFT-TISSUE INFECTIONS (12 STATIONS)
topic: Diabetic Foot Ulcer — Healing & Perfusion Assessment
stem: A 59-year-old diabetic man is reviewed in the surgical outpatient clinic during follow-up of a dorsal foot ulcer shown in the photograph. Before planning reconstructive coverage, which pair of assessments most reliably evaluates arterial perfusion of the foot?
options: 10 g Semmes-Weinstein monofilament and 128 Hz tuning fork testing
Trendelenburg tourniquet test and Perthes clinical test
Plain foot radiograph and serum C-reactive protein level
Superficial wound swab culture and glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c)
Pedal pulse palpation and hand-held Doppler / Ankle-Brachial Index
optionRationales: Incorrect: Monofilament and 128 Hz tuning fork tests assess peripheral neuropathy (protective sensation and vibration), not arterial blood flow.
Incorrect: Trendelenburg and Perthes tests evaluate superficial venous incompetence and deep venous patency in varicose veins, not arterial perfusion.
Incorrect: Radiographs and CRP detect underlying osteomyelitis or systemic inflammation rather than quantifying arterial inflow.
Incorrect: Swab culture and HbA1c reflect colonisation and glycaemic control rather than limb perfusion.

Correct: The ulcer shows healthy pink/beefy-red granulation tissue and contracting margins; arterial perfusion is evaluated clinically by palpating dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses and objectively using hand-held Doppler / Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI) or arterial Duplex ultrasound.
clinicalPearl: Healthy pink/beefy-red granulation tissue with contracting epithelial edges signals active ulcer healing, while dorsalis pedis/posterior tibial pulse palpation plus Doppler ABI confirms adequate perfusion for reconstruction.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Assess vascular status of lower-limb ulcers by examining pedal pulses, capillary refill, and Doppler/Duplex flow before surgical closure or grafting.

sourceStation.title: Healing Diabetic Foot Ulcer & Perfusion Assessment
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
12. This is a diabetic foot ulcer.
12.1 List two (02) features to indicate this ulcer is healing.
12.2 Write two (02) methods to assess the perfusion of the foot.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (12.1) Healing features: Healthy pink/beefy-red granulation tissue, absence of slough/purulence/cellulitis, contracting wound edges with epithelialisation rim. (12.2) Assessing perfusion: (a) Palpation of pedal pulses (dorsalis pedis & posterior tibial) & capillary refill time; (b) Hand-held Doppler / Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI) or Arterial Duplex ultrasound.

domain: 2.5 VASCULAR, DIABETIC FOOT & SOFT-TISSUE INFECTIONS (12 STATIONS)
stem: A 40-year-old farmer is admitted to the surgical ward with high fever and a painful, acutely expanding erythematous skin lesion on his leg, as shown. Blood cultures are obtained. Which initial inpatient antibiotic and supportive management plan is most appropriate?
options: Oral terbinafine therapy with occlusive topical corticosteroid
Intravenous metronidazole monotherapy with warm fomentation
Intravenous benzylpenicillin with limb elevation and analgesia
Immediate surgical debridement and below-knee amputation
Oral fluconazole with graduated elastic compression stockings
optionRationales: Incorrect: Antifungals and topical steroids do not treat acute bacterial dermal infection and steroids can worsen bacterial spread.
Incorrect: Metronidazole targets obligate anaerobes and is ineffective against Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus.

Correct: The sharply demarcated fiery-red plaque represents erysipelas (typically Streptococcus pyogenes, occasionally Staphylococcus aureus), managed with IV benzylpenicillin/penicillin G (or cephalosporin/clindamycin/erythromycin if allergic), limb elevation, local cooling/wet dressings if ulcerated, and analgesia.
Incorrect: Amputation is indicated only for unsalvageable gangrene or life-threatening necrotising sepsis, never uncomplicated erysipelas.
Incorrect: Fluconazole treats fungal disease and tight compression is avoided during acute painful infective inflammation.
clinicalPearl: First-line ward therapy for acute erysipelas is IV benzylpenicillin (Penicillin G) or a beta-lactam/clindamycin in penicillin allergy, combined with limb elevation, antipyretics, and local wound care.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Treat acute erysipelas with crystalline penicillin (or cephalosporin, clindamycin, or erythromycin) alongside limb elevation and symptomatic analgesia.

sourceStation.title: Erysipelas in a Farmer

(5.3) Management: (1) Antibiotics (Crystalline penicillin / Penicillin G, cephalosporin, clindamycin, or erythromycin); (2) Local wound care (saline wet dressings if ulcerated, cold compresses, limb elevation); (3) Symptomatic analgesia/antipyretics + surgical debridement if necrotic.

domain: 2.5 VASCULAR, DIABETIC FOOT & SOFT-TISSUE INFECTIONS (12 STATIONS)
topic: Dorsum Foot Ulcer — Slough vs Granulation Tissue
stem: A 65-year-old man with diabetes mellitus and peripheral arterial disease presents with a chronic wound on the dorsum of the foot, with zones A and B marked as shown. Which option correctly identifies the tissue types labelled A and B?
options: A = Devitalised fibrinous slough; B = Granulation tissue
A = Granulation tissue; B = Necrotic black eschar
A = Epithelialising wound edge; B = Exposed extensor tendon
A = Hyperkeratotic neuropathic callus; B = Subcutaneous adipose
A = Exposed metatarsal cortex; B = Purulent abscess cavity
optionRationales: Correct: Zone A points to yellowish devitalised fibrinous/necrotic slough adherent to the wound bed (requiring debridement), while Zone B points to healthy red vascularised granulation tissue.
Incorrect: Granulation tissue is beefy red (Zone B), whereas yellowish fibrinous material (Zone A) is slough rather than black eschar.
Incorrect: Epithelialisation appears as a pale pink/translucent advancing rim at the skin margin rather than central yellow fibrinous exudate.
Incorrect: Neuropathic callus forms thickened hyperkeratotic skin surrounding pressure points on the plantar foot rather than moist yellow wound-bed slough.
Incorrect: Neither cortical bone nor a deep fluctuant abscess pocket corresponds to these superficial wound-bed zones.
clinicalPearl: Distinguishing yellow devitalised slough (which impedes healing and requires debridement) from beefy-red granulation tissue (indicating healthy vascular bed ready for contraction or grafting) guides ulcer care.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Surgical wound bed assessment differentiates removable yellow necrotic slough from healthy vascular granulation tissue prior to dressings or skin grafting.

sourceStation.title: Dorsum Foot Ulcer — Slough vs Granulation Tissue
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
16. 65-year-old patient presented with wound on the dorsum of the foot (zones A and B labelled).
16.1 List 3 underlying causes.
16.2 Name the areas labelled A & B.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (16.1) Causes: Diabetes mellitus (neuro-ischaemic), Peripheral arterial disease (ischaemic ulcer), Venous insufficiency / trauma / vasculitis. (16.2) Areas: A = Slough (necrotic/fibrinous devitalised tissue); B = Granulation tissue.

domain: 2.5 VASCULAR, DIABETIC FOOT & SOFT-TISSUE INFECTIONS (12 STATIONS)
stem: A 70-year-old man who underwent femoro-popliteal bypass surgery 7 days ago is readmitted with low-grade fever and the wound appearance shown. Which post-operative complication and most frequent causative organism are represented?
options: Primary arterial graft thrombosis; Streptococcus pneumoniae
Post-operative lymphocele fistula; Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Suture hypersensitivity granuloma; Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Surgical site infection (SSI); Staphylococcus aureus
Acute ischaemic flap necrosis; Clostridium perfringens
optionRationales: Incorrect: Graft thrombosis presents with acute limb ischaemia (pain, pallor, pulselessness) rather than purulent wound dehiscence at day 7.
Incorrect: A lymphocele leaks clear straw-coloured lymphatic fluid rather than thick purulent slough with surrounding inflammatory erythema.
Incorrect: Foreign-body suture reactions are indolent and sterile rather than acute purulent breakdown 1 week post-op.

Correct: Wound dehiscence with purulent exudate, slough, and peri-incisional erythema at day 7 is a classic surgical site infection (SSI), most commonly caused by skin flora such as Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) or S. epidermidis.
Incorrect: Clostridial myonecrosis presents hyperacutely within 24–48 hours with crepitus and severe systemic toxicity rather than a day-7 groin wound infection.
clinicalPearl: Groin incisions for vascular bypass carry high SSI risk (skin folds, seroma, distal ischaemia); prevention relies on the WHO SSI bundle (timely IV antibiotic prophylaxis, normothermia, appropriate hair removal, and glycaemic control).

guideCitation.keyPoint: The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist SSI bundle mandates timely antibiotic prophylaxis, patient warming, proper hair removal, and glycaemic control to prevent surgical site infection.

sourceStation.title: Post-Operative Surgical Site Infection (Femoro-Popliteal Bypass)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
02. A 70-year-old male who has undergone femoro-popliteal bypass surgery is admitted to the ward after 7 days.
2.1 Identify this complication.
2.2 What is the most likely cause?
2.3 State one likely organism responsible.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (2.1) Surgical site infection (SSI) / Prosthetic or vein graft wound infection. (2.2) Cause: Bacterial wound contamination (skin flora entry perioperatively, exacerbated by poor distal perfusion/seroma/haematoma in groin crease). (2.3) Organism: Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA; also Staphylococcus epidermidis or Gram-negatives).

domain: 2.5 VASCULAR, DIABETIC FOOT & SOFT-TISSUE INFECTIONS (12 STATIONS)
stem: A 64-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes presents to the emergency surgical unit with the forefoot appearance shown, accompanied by fever and foul-smelling discharge. What is the diagnosis, and which urgent bedside assessment is essential before surgical intervention?
options: Dry (aseptic) gangrene; await spontaneous auto-amputation without antibiotics
Tinea pedis with intertrigo; prescribe topical clotrimazole cream only
Acute gouty podagra; initiate oral colchicine and allopurinol
Charcot neuroarthropathy; immobilise immediately in a total-contact cast
Wet (infected) gangrene; assess pedal pulses and proximal cellulitis or crepitus
optionRationales: Incorrect: Moist, swollen, sloughing digits with proximal erythema and malodorous discharge indicate superadded infection (wet gangrene), which rapidly spreads if left for auto-amputation.
Incorrect: Superficial dermatophyte infection does not cause full-thickness tissue necrosis of the toes or systemic sepsis.
Incorrect: Gout causes acute crystal arthritis of a joint without blackened digital necrosis or foul exudate.
Incorrect: Charcot arthropathy causes rocker-bottom midfoot collapse without moist gangrenous slough; casting an actively infected foot is dangerous.

Correct: Swollen, moist, necrotic 1st–3rd toes with sloughing skin and proximal erythema represent wet (infected) gangrene; urgently check pedal pulses (DP/PT), line of demarcation, proximal spreading cellulitis/crepitus, and protective sensation alongside antibiotics and surgical debridement/amputation.
clinicalPearl: Unlike dry gangrene, wet gangrene is an infective surgical emergency with a poorly defined boundary and rapid proximal spread; always check pedal pulses, crepitus, and proximal cellulitis before urgent debridement or amputation.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Differentiate aseptic dry gangrene from infected wet gangrene by looking for oedema, foul exudate, proximal cellulitis, and crepitus while assessing pedal pulses.

sourceStation.title: Wet Gangrene of Toes
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
3.1 What is the diagnosis?
3.2 Write down two other features of the foot that you will look for.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (3.1) Wet (infected) gangrene of the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd toes. (3.2) Other features to check: Pedal pulses (dorsalis pedis & posterior tibial), Line of demarcation / proximal spreading cellulitis & crepitus, Skin temperature & capillary refill, Loss of protective sensation (monofilament testing).

domain: 2.5 VASCULAR, DIABETIC FOOT & SOFT-TISSUE INFECTIONS (12 STATIONS)
stem: A 46-year-old teacher presents with aching lower limbs at the end of the workday and the leg appearance shown. Which investigation is the gold-standard modality to evaluate this condition and guide definitive treatment?
options: Ascending conventional contrast venography
Venous Duplex ultrasound scan (colour Doppler)
Resting Ankle-Brachial Pressure Index (ABPI) alone
CT pulmonary angiography of the lower limbs
Plain anteroposterior radiographs of both calves
optionRationales: Incorrect: Invasive contrast venography has been superseded by non-invasive Duplex ultrasound and is reserved for select complex deep venous reconstructions.

Correct: Dilated, tortuous superficial lower-limb veins represent varicose veins (chronic venous insufficiency); Venous Duplex ultrasound (colour Doppler) is the investigation of choice to map saphenofemoral/saphenopopliteal junction incompetence, perforators, and exclude DVT.
Incorrect: ABPI assesses arterial inflow (useful before compression therapy) but cannot map venous valve reflux or deep venous patency.
Incorrect: CT pulmonary angiography evaluates pulmonary arteries for embolism rather than superficial lower-limb venous reflux.
Incorrect: Plain radiographs cannot visualise superficial venous valves or incompetent junctions.
clinicalPearl: Venous Duplex ultrasound is the gold-standard investigation for varicose veins because it non-invasively maps reflux at the SFJ/SPJ and perforators while confirming a patent deep venous system.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Evaluate varicose veins (managed conservatively, via sclerotherapy, endovenous ablation, or ligation) using colour Duplex ultrasound to localise venous incompetence and exclude DVT.

sourceStation.title: Varicose Veins & Venous Duplex Ultrasound
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
4.1 What is your diagnosis?
4.2 What is the best investigation modality to identify the above diagnosis?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (4.1) Varicose veins (lower limb chronic venous insufficiency). (4.2) Best investigation: Venous Duplex Ultrasound scan (Colour Doppler) (identifies saphenofemoral/saphenopopliteal junction incompetence, perforators, and excludes DVT).

domain: 2.5 VASCULAR, DIABETIC FOOT & SOFT-TISSUE INFECTIONS (12 STATIONS)
stem: A 66-year-old man attending the surgical clinic has the healed chest and lower limb scars shown. Which prior operation did he undergo, and what accounts for the linear scar on his leg?
options: Aortic valve replacement; anterior tibial artery cannulation
Transhiatal oesophagectomy; sural nerve graft harvesting
Thymectomy for myasthenia; femoral vein transposition
Coronary artery bypass grafting; long saphenous vein harvesting
Median sternotomy biopsy; Trendelenburg varicose vein stripping
optionRationales: Incorrect: Isolated aortic valve replacement via sternotomy does not require harvesting a long medial lower-limb conduit.
Incorrect: Oesophagectomy uses abdominal/thoracic/cervical incisions rather than a median sternotomy and medial saphenous vein harvest.
Incorrect: Thymectomy does not involve harvesting a long leg vein for bypass conduits.

Correct: The midline chest scar represents a median sternotomy for coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG), and the medial leg scar represents harvesting of the long (great) saphenous vein as an autologous bypass conduit.
Incorrect: Trendelenburg varicose vein surgery involves a groin crease incision rather than a full-length harvest scar paired with a median sternotomy.
clinicalPearl: A healed median sternotomy scar paired with a long medial leg (or forearm radial) scar is a classic surgical OSCE spotter indicating prior CABG with great saphenous vein conduit harvesting.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Patients with prior ischaemic heart disease/CABG require careful preoperative cardiac risk stratification (NYHA class, ECG, ECHO, and antiplatelet review) before non-cardiac surgery.

sourceStation.title: Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG) Scars
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
2.1 Name the surgery that is likely to have been performed on this patient.
2.2 What could be the reason for the scar in the leg?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (2.1) Coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) via median sternotomy. (2.2) Reason for leg scar: Long (great) saphenous vein harvesting used as autologous venous conduit for coronary bypass grafts.

domain: 2.6 UROLOGY & RENAL IMAGING (3 STATIONS)
topic: Persistent Microscopic Haematuria in Older Adult
stem: A previously healthy 64-year-old man presents with intermittent lower abdominal pain. Two urine full reports repeated 1 week apart consistently show acidic turbid urine with nil protein or sugar, 2–3 pus cells/hpf, 20–30 RBCs/hpf, and calcium oxalate crystals (++). While urolithiasis is likely, which serious underlying condition must also be actively excluded in this patient?
options: Urothelial (bladder) or renal cell carcinoma
Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
Orthostatic (postural) benign proteinuria
Diabetic nephropathy with nephrotic syndrome
Acute asymptomatic bacteriuria of elderly males
optionRationales: Correct: Persistent non-visible (microscopic) haematuria (20–30 RBCs/hpf) in a 64-year-old man, even with calcium oxalate crystalluria suggesting urolithiasis, mandates excluding urological malignancy (bladder transitional cell carcinoma or renal cell carcinoma) via imaging and cystoscopy.
Incorrect: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis features dysmorphic RBC casts, proteinuria, oedema, and hypertension rather than isolated crystalluria with nil protein.
Incorrect: Orthostatic proteinuria produces transient proteinuria in upright adolescents, not persistent haematuria with negative urinary protein.
Incorrect: Diabetic nephropathy presents with progressive albuminuria/proteinuria and normal RBC counts rather than isolated microscopic haematuria.
Incorrect: Pus cells are minimal (2–3/hpf) and asymptomatic bacteriuria does not explain persistent microscopic haematuria in a 64-year-old.
clinicalPearl: In any patient aged > 40–50 years with persistent microscopic haematuria, always investigate to exclude urological malignancy (CT urogram/USS + cystoscopy) even when urinary crystals suggest a stone.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Perform urinalysis preoperatively—especially before urological interventions—and evaluate persistent haematuria thoroughly for urolithiasis and underlying urothelial malignancy.

sourceStation.title: Persistent Microscopic Haematuria with Calcium Oxalate Crystalluria

domain: 2.6 UROLOGY & RENAL IMAGING (3 STATIONS)
stem: A 60-year-old man presents to the urology clinic with a 2-month history of poor urinary stream, hesitancy, and straining. His clinic trace (Qmax 7 mL/s, voiding time 58 s, voided volume 297 mL) is shown alongside a normal reference curve. Which investigation and diagnosis best account for this flat plateau pattern?
options: Cystometrogram; neurogenic detrusor overactivity
Retrograde urethrogram; acute bacterial prostatitis
Uroflowmetry; fixed urethral stricture obstruction
Micturating cystourethrogram; primary vesicoureteric reflux
Intravenous urogram; distal ureteric calculus
optionRationales: Incorrect: Cystometry measures intravesical pressure against bladder filling volume rather than urinary flow rate (mL/s) over time.
Incorrect: A retrograde urethrogram is a contrast radiograph of the urethra rather than a flow-rate curve, and acute prostatitis is not the classic cause of a fixed box-shaped flow plateau.

Correct: The graph is a uroflowmetry trace demonstrating severely reduced Qmax (7 mL/s; normal > 15 mL/s), prolonged voiding (58 s), and a flat box-like plateau characteristic of fixed bladder outlet obstruction from a urethral stricture (risking retention, recurrent UTIs, bladder diverticula, and obstructive uropathy).
Incorrect: An MCUG is a fluoroscopic voiding radiograph used mainly to grade reflux or posterior urethral valves rather than a flow-volume curve.
Incorrect: An IVU is a contrast renal tract radiograph and a ureteric calculus causes renal colic rather than a flat urethral flow plateau.
clinicalPearl: A flattened, low-amplitude ('box-shaped') uroflowmetry curve with Qmax < 10 mL/s and prolonged voiding time classically indicates fixed urethral stricture; untreated obstruction leads to urinary retention, UTIs, trabeculation, and bilateral hydronephrosis.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Urethral stricture is a classic late complication of urethral trauma or catheterisation that produces chronic bladder outlet obstruction and obstructive uropathy if untreated.

topic: Non-Contrast CT KUB — Left Ureteric Calculus
stem: A 42-year-old man presents to the emergency unit with severe left-sided loin-to-groin colicky pain and microscopic haematuria. A coronal slice from his diagnostic imaging study is shown. Which modality and key abnormalities are demonstrated?
options: Non-contrast CT KUB; left ureteric calculus with left hydronephrosis
Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen; left renal cell carcinoma with vein thrombus
Intravenous urogram; right pelviureteric junction obstruction
Non-contrast CT KUB; bilateral nephrocalcinosis with medullary sponge kidney
CT renal angiogram; left renal artery aneurysm with retroperitoneal bleed
optionRationales: Correct: This coronal non-contrast CT KUB (no intravascular contrast in aorta or renal vessels) demonstrates a bright hyperdense calculus in the left proximal ureter causing proximal left hydronephrosis and hydroureter.
Incorrect: The aorta and renal parenchyma lack intravenous contrast enhancement, and there is a small focal calcified ureteric stone rather than a solid renal tumour.
Incorrect: This is cross-sectional CT imaging rather than a plain-film intravenous urogram, and the dilated collecting system is on the left side.
Incorrect: Bilateral parenchymal medullary calcifications are absent; a single discrete obstructing calculus sits in the left ureter.
Incorrect: No intravenous contrast bolus is present for angiography and there is no retroperitoneal haematoma.
clinicalPearl: Non-contrast CT KUB is the gold-standard investigation for acute ureteric colic (sensitivity > 95%), identifying even radiolucent urate stones alongside hydronephrosis and perinephric fat stranding.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Suspected acute obstructing ureteric calculus is confirmed with non-contrast CT KUB, assessing stone site/size and degree of proximal hydronephrosis.

domain: 2.7 SURGICAL TUBES, CATHETERS, SUTURES, IMAGING & INSTRUMENTS (13 STATIONS)
stem: The surgical tube shown is prepared for emergency thoracic placement. Which anatomical site defines the 'safe triangle' for its insertion, and what is a primary clinical indication for its use?
options: 2nd intercostal space mid-clavicular line; acute pericardial tamponade
7th intercostal space paravertebral line; cardiogenic pulmonary oedema
Subxiphoid epigastric notch; pneumoperitoneum from perforated ulcer
5th intercostal space anterior to the mid-axillary line; pneumothorax or haemothorax
Suprasternal notch above the manubrium; subglottic tracheal stenosis
optionRationales: Incorrect: The 2nd ICS mid-clavicular line is used for emergency needle decompression of tension pneumothorax, whereas formal ICD tubes are placed in the lateral 5th ICS safe triangle (and never for pericardial tamponade).
Incorrect: Inserting a drain at the 7th ICS risks diaphragmatic, hepatic, or splenic perforation, and pulmonary oedema is managed medically rather than by chest drainage.
Incorrect: Subxiphoid access is used for pericardiocentesis rather than pleural drainage.

Correct: This is an intercostal drainage (ICD) chest tube (24–34 Fr) inserted via blunt dissection just over the upper border of the 5th rib within the safe triangle (5th ICS anterior to mid-axillary line, lateral to pectoralis major, anterior to latissimus dorsi) for pneumothorax, haemothorax, pleural effusion, or empyema.
Incorrect: The suprasternal notch sits over the trachea and great vessels rather than the pleural space.
clinicalPearl: Insert chest drains via blunt dissection using curved artery (Roberts) forceps along the upper border of the 5th rib (safe triangle) to avoid the intercostal neurovascular bundle running along the inferior rib groove.

guideCitation.guideTitle: NG Tube, IC Tube & Urinary Catheter Surgery OSCE Guide
guideCitation.keyPoint: Position the patient at 45 degrees with arm abducted behind the head, incise at the upper border of the 5th rib within the safe triangle, and connect the 24–34 Fr ICD tube to an underwater seal.

domain: 2.7 SURGICAL TUBES, CATHETERS, SUTURES, IMAGING & INSTRUMENTS (13 STATIONS)
stem: A vascular surgeon is closing a longitudinal common femoral arteriotomy after performing an emergency embolectomy. Which suture material and gauge provides optimal non-absorbable monofilament strength with minimal tissue drag for this arterial repair?
options: Braided black silk suture 1-0
Polypropylene (Prolene) 5-0
Chromic catgut suture 2-0
Braided polyglactin (Vicryl) 1-0
Loop polydioxanone (PDS) 1-0
optionRationales: Incorrect: Braided silk provokes pronounced tissue reaction, loses tensile strength over time, and drags through delicate arterial walls.

Correct: Vascular anastomoses and arterial repairs (such as femoral arteriotomy closure) require a fine non-absorbable monofilament suture—specifically Polypropylene (Prolene) 5-0 or 6-0—for smooth passage and permanent tensile support (whereas loop PDS/nylon is used for mass abdominal closure and Vicryl/PDS 3-0 for small bowel).
Incorrect: Catgut is a natural rapidly absorbable suture with intense inflammatory reactivity and high failure risk in arterial closure.
Incorrect: Heavy 1-0 braided Vicryl is absorbable and causes excessive tissue drag, making it unsuitable for fine arterial repairs.
Incorrect: Heavy 1-0 loop PDS is designed for mass closure of the abdominal wall fascia rather than delicate peripheral arterial suturing.
clinicalPearl: Match surgical sutures by tissue healing time and drag: loop PDS/Nylon for mass abdominal closure, Prolene 5-0/6-0 for arterial repair, Prolene/Ethibond 3-0/4-0 for flexor tendons, and Vicryl/PDS 3-0 for small bowel.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Polypropylene (Prolene) is a synthetic non-absorbable monofilament offering minimal tissue drag and permanent tensile strength for vascular and tendon repairs.

(4) Small intestine anastomosis: Polyglactin (Vicryl) 3-0 or Polydioxanone (PDS) 3-0/4-0 (absorbable).

domain: 2.7 SURGICAL TUBES, CATHETERS, SUTURES, IMAGING & INSTRUMENTS (13 STATIONS)
stem: A 65-year-old man presents with painful acute urinary retention. Prior to inserting the medical device shown via the urethra, which topical lubricant/analgesic agent should be instilled intraurethrally and left for 3–5 minutes?
options: 10% povidone-iodine aqueous solution
70% isopropyl alcohol antiseptic spray
0.5% bupivacaine plain injection fluid
White soft paraffin without local anaesthetic
2% lignocaine (lidocaine) water-soluble gel
optionRationales: Incorrect: Povidone-iodine is used externally to cleanse the urethral meatus and glans prior to draping, not instilled intraurethrally for analgesia.
Incorrect: Alcohol causes severe chemical mucosal burning and must never be instilled into the urethra.
Incorrect: Aqueous injectable bupivacaine provides no lubrication and lacks urethral mucosal dwell time.
Incorrect: Plain paraffin provides no local anaesthesia and oil-based lubricants can damage latex Foley balloons.

Correct: The image shows a two-way Foley urinary catheter; in male catheterisation, 2% lignocaine water-soluble gel is instilled intraurethrally (waiting 3–5 minutes before insertion) to provide both mucosal analgesia and lubrication.
clinicalPearl: For male Foley catheterisation (typically 14–16 Fr), cleanse with povidone-iodine under sterile non-touch technique, instil 2% lignocaine gel, wait 3–5 minutes, confirm urine flow before balloon inflation, and always reduce the prepuce afterward.

guideCitation.keyPoint: During male Foley catheterisation, empty a full tube of 2% lignocaine gel into the urethra and wait 3–5 minutes before atraumatic insertion.

domain: 2.7 SURGICAL TUBES, CATHETERS, SUTURES, IMAGING & INSTRUMENTS (13 STATIONS)
stem: A 54-year-old man is admitted with persistent bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, and tinkling bowel sounds secondary to adhesive small bowel obstruction. Which tube is indicated for immediate gastric decompression, and which injury constitutes a strict contraindication to inserting it via the nasal route?
options: Foley catheter; benign prostatic hyperplasia
Endotracheal tube; uncomplicated rib fracture
Ryles (nasogastric) tube; base of skull fracture
Sengstaken-Blakemore tube; peptic ulcer disease
Flatus rectal tube; internal haemorrhoids
optionRationales: Incorrect: A Foley catheter drains the urinary bladder rather than decompressing the stomach.
Incorrect: An endotracheal tube secures the trachea for ventilation rather than draining obstructed gastric fluid.

Correct: A Ryles (nasogastric) tube is used for gastric decompression (bowel obstruction, ileus, post-operative), enteral feeding, and gastric aspiration/lavage; nasal insertion is strictly contraindicated in base of skull fractures due to the risk of intracranial tube misplacement through the cribriform plate.
Incorrect: A Sengstaken-Blakemore balloon tamponade tube is reserved for refractory oesophageal variceal bleeding.
Incorrect: A flatus tube relieves distal colonic/sigmoid volvulus gas rather than upper gastrointestinal obstruction.
clinicalPearl: In basal skull fracture (raccoon eyes, Battle sign, CSF rhinorrhoea/otorrhoea), never insert a nasogastric or nasotracheal tube nasally—use the orogastric route if gastric decompression is required.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Ryles NG tubes are indicated for gastric decompression in intestinal obstruction and enteral feeding, but are contraindicated nasally in base of skull fractures.

domain: 2.7 SURGICAL TUBES, CATHETERS, SUTURES, IMAGING & INSTRUMENTS (13 STATIONS)
stem: A malnourished surgical patient with a high-output enterocutaneous fistula requires prolonged total parenteral nutrition (TPN) via a central venous catheter. Which venous access site is preferred over the femoral route to minimise catheter-related infection, and which acute mechanical complication is most classically associated with subclavian cannulation?
options: Great saphenous vein; deep vein thrombosis
External jugular vein; brachial artery pseudoaneurysm
Internal jugular or subclavian vein; pneumothorax
Basilic cubital vein; retroperitoneal haematoma
Femoral vein; thoracic duct chylothorax
optionRationales: Incorrect: The great saphenous vein is a peripheral lower-limb vein unsuitable for central hyperosmolar TPN infusion.
Incorrect: The external jugular vein often has valves and tortuous entry into the subclavian vein and is distant from the brachial artery.

Correct: The internal jugular and subclavian veins are preferred CVC sites for TPN (avoiding femoral lines due to higher infection and thrombosis risk); immediate cannulation complications include pneumothorax/haemothorax (highest with subclavian access), arterial puncture, air embolism, arrhythmias, and thoracic duct injury (left-sided).
Incorrect: A basilic vein PICC line does not cause retroperitoneal haematoma, which complicates high femoral/iliac punctures.
Incorrect: The femoral route is avoided for TPN because of infection risk, and thoracic duct injury occurs during left internal jugular or left subclavian cannulation.
clinicalPearl: Use Seldinger technique under ultrasound guidance for IJV/subclavian CVC placement for TPN or irritant infusions (inotropes, KCl, amiodarone), and obtain a post-procedure CXR to confirm tip position (cavoatrial junction) and exclude pneumothorax.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Central venous access for TPN uses the internal jugular or subclavian veins via Seldinger technique; immediate complications include pneumothorax, arterial puncture, arrhythmia, air embolism, and left thoracic duct injury.

Cannulation complications: Pneumothorax/haemothorax, Arterial puncture / haematoma, Air embolism, Cardiac arrhythmia, Injury to brachial plexus/thoracic duct, Catheter malposition. (Late: CRBSI/infection, venous thrombosis.)

domain: 2.7 SURGICAL TUBES, CATHETERS, SUTURES, IMAGING & INSTRUMENTS (13 STATIONS)
stem: After inserting the tube shown into an adult surgical patient for enteral feeding, which bedside test is the recommended first-line method to confirm correct gastric placement before commencing feeds?
options: Injecting 10 mL of air while auscultating over the epigastrium
Immersing the proximal tube end in water to exclude air bubbles
Measuring the external tube length remaining outside the nostril
Asking the patient to speak clearly and swallow sips of water
Aspirating gastric fluid and confirming pH <= 5.5 on indicator paper
optionRationales: Incorrect: The epigastric 'whoosh' auscultation test is unreliable because air insufflated into a malpositioned bronchial or oesophageal tube can still be transmitted across the diaphragm.
Incorrect: Underwater bubbling checks lack sensitivity and specificity—false negatives occur when pleural/bronchial tips occlude against mucosa, and gastric gas can bubble.
Incorrect: External tube length cannot detect coiling in the pharynx or accidental tracheal advancement.
Incorrect: Intact phonation does not exclude subglottic/bronchial misplacement, especially with small-bore tubes or depressed airway reflexes.

Correct: Aspirating gastric contents and testing with pH indicator paper (confirming acidic pH <= 5.5) is the gold-standard first-line bedside confirmation before initial feeding and prior to every subsequent feed.
clinicalPearl: Always confirm NG position on initial insertion, before every feed, and after vomiting/coughing/desaturation using aspirate pH <= 5.5 first, proceeding to chest/upper abdominal X-ray if no aspirate or pH > 5.5.

guideCitation.guideTitle: NG Tube, IC Tube & Urinary Catheter Surgery OSCE Guide
guideCitation.keyPoint: Confirm NG tube placement using a 60 mL syringe and pH litmus strip (acidic aspirate) or X-ray; measure insertion length from philtrum to tragus to xiphisternum and never reinsert a guidewire in situ.

domain: 2.7 SURGICAL TUBES, CATHETERS, SUTURES, IMAGING & INSTRUMENTS (13 STATIONS)
topic: Suture Classification — Synthetic Absorbable for Gut
stem: During an exploratory laparotomy and small bowel resection, a trainee must choose among three available suture materials: black silk, polyethylene, and polyglycolic acid. Which suture is synthetic and absorbable, making it most appropriate for suturing the gut mucosa and bowel wall?
options: Polyglycolic acid
Black silk
Polyethylene
Polypropylene
Monofilament nylon
optionRationales: Correct: Polyglycolic acid (Dexon) is a synthetic absorbable suture appropriate for gut mucosa/anastomosis (whereas black silk is braided natural non-absorbable used for skin/ties, and polyethylene/nylon/polypropylene are non-absorbable monofilaments).
Incorrect: Black silk is a braided, natural, non-absorbable suture that elicits high tissue reactivity and should not be buried in bowel anastomoses.
Incorrect: Polyethylene is a synthetic non-absorbable monofilament used for skin or fascial closure rather than gut mucosa.
Incorrect: Polypropylene (Prolene) is a synthetic non-absorbable monofilament suited to vascular or fascial repairs.
Incorrect: Nylon (polyamide) is a synthetic non-absorbable monofilament used mainly for skin or abdominal wall closure.
clinicalPearl: Bowel anastomoses heal rapidly and require synthetic absorbable sutures (polyglycolic acid, polyglactin/Vicryl, or polydioxanone/PDS), whereas skin and vascular repairs typically use non-absorbable monofilaments.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Synthetic absorbable sutures include polyglactin (Vicryl), polyglycolic acid, poliglecaprone (Monocryl), and polydioxanone (PDS), whereas nylon and Prolene are non-absorbable monofilaments.

domain: 2.7 SURGICAL TUBES, CATHETERS, SUTURES, IMAGING & INSTRUMENTS (13 STATIONS)
stem: A 32-year-old woman with acute upper abdominal pain is scheduled to undergo the cross-sectional imaging investigation shown. Before proceeding with intravenous contrast administration, which trio of clinical enquiries is most essential to exclude radiation and contrast hazards?
options: Metallic cardiac pacemaker, cochlear implant, and claustrophobia
Pregnancy status/LMP, prior contrast/iodine allergy, and renal disease
24-hour solid food fasting, aspirin therapy, and previous appendicectomy
Recent tetanus immunisation, blood group, and lactose intolerance
Contact lens wear, inhaled corticosteroid use, and mild ankle oedema
optionRationales: Incorrect: Metallic implants, pacemakers, and severe claustrophobia are primary pre-MRI safety checks rather than key contraindications for CT scanning.

Correct: This is a Computed Tomography (CT) scan; essential pre-contrast history includes pregnancy status/LMP (ionising radiation risk in childbearing women), allergies (iodinated contrast/asthma/atopy), and renal disease (contrast-induced nephropathy risk—check baseline eGFR/creatinine and metformin use).
Incorrect: Routine 24-hour fasting and stopping aspirin are unnecessary for diagnostic CT imaging.
Incorrect: Blood group, tetanus status, and lactose intolerance do not alter CT radiation or contrast safety.
Incorrect: Contact lenses and inhaled steroids do not contraindicate CT scanning with IV contrast.
clinicalPearl: Before every contrast-enhanced CT scan, always screen the '4 checks': Pregnancy/LMP (ionising radiation), Renal function (eGFR/creatinine), Allergies (contrast/iodine/asthma), and Metformin use.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Pre-investigation surgical preparation includes baseline renal function (U&Es/creatinine), drug review (metformin), allergy checks, and pregnancy verification before radiological studies.

domain: 2.7 SURGICAL TUBES, CATHETERS, SUTURES, IMAGING & INSTRUMENTS (13 STATIONS)
stem: Following emergency airway management in a trauma patient using the cuffed airway device shown, which finding provides the gold-standard objective confirmation of correct tracheal placement?
options: Condensation mist appearing inside the lumen during expiration
Absence of gurgling sounds on auscultation over the epigastrium
Symmetric bilateral chest wall rise during manual bag ventilation
Continuous waveform capnography showing persistent end-tidal CO2
Equal vesicular breath sounds heard over both lung apices
optionRationales: Incorrect: Tube misting can occur transiently even after oesophageal intubation due to warm humidified gastric gas and is unreliable.
Incorrect: Absent epigastric gurgling supports tracheal placement only indirectly and does not reliably rule out supraglottic or oesophageal malposition.
Incorrect: Chest wall movement can be obscured in obesity or mimicked by gastric insufflation and must not replace objective confirmation.

Correct: The image shows a cuffed endotracheal tube (ETT); continuous waveform capnography demonstrating sustained end-tidal CO2 (ETCO2) over multiple breaths is the gold-standard objective confirmation of tracheal intubation (supplemented by bilateral chest rise, equal air entry, and absent epigastric gurgling).
Incorrect: Auscultation can transmit breath sounds falsely in thin chests or fail to detect right mainstem intubation if compared poorly; waveform capnography remains the gold standard.
clinicalPearl: Never rely solely on condensation misting or auscultation after ETT insertion; continuous waveform capnography ('no trace = wrong place') is mandatory to confirm tracheal placement.

guideCitation.keyPoint: An endotracheal tube features a 15 mm universal connector, radiopaque line, and inflatable cuff (preventing air leak and aspiration); confirm placement immediately via ETCO2 capnography, chest rise, and bilateral auscultation.

(b) Confirmation: (1) Continuous waveform capnography (ETCO₂ detector) — gold standard; (2) Bilateral equal chest rise and equal air entry on auscultation over both lung fields + absent gurgling over epigastrium; (3) Direct visualisation passing vocal cords & tube misting.

domain: 2.7 SURGICAL TUBES, CATHETERS, SUTURES, IMAGING & INSTRUMENTS (13 STATIONS)
stem: Based on standard surgical suture classifications, a surgeon selects polydioxanone (PDS) for mass closure of a midline laparotomy fascia. Which set of characteristics accurately describes polydioxanone?
options: Natural, braided, non-absorbable suture
Synthetic, monofilament, absorbable suture
Synthetic, braided, rapidly absorbable suture
Natural, monofilament, rapidly absorbable suture
Synthetic, monofilament, non-absorbable suture
optionRationales: Incorrect: Natural braided non-absorbable describes black silk rather than polydioxanone.

Correct: Polydioxanone (PDS) is a synthetic, monofilament, slowly absorbable suture ideal for anterior abdominal wall mass closure and bowel anastomosis (unlike braided polyglactin or non-absorbable monofilament nylon).
Incorrect: Polyglactin (Vicryl) and polyglycolic acid are synthetic braided absorbable sutures, whereas PDS is monofilament with prolonged absorption (~180 days).
Incorrect: Plain or chromic catgut is a natural absorbable suture, not synthetic PDS.
Incorrect: Nylon and polypropylene (Prolene) are synthetic monofilament non-absorbable sutures, whereas PDS undergoes eventual hydrolysis.
clinicalPearl: Polydioxanone (PDS) combines low-drag monofilament handling with prolonged absorbable tensile strength (~6 weeks+ retention), making it first-line for laparotomy mass closure and bowel anastomosis.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Polydioxanone (PDS) and poliglecaprone (Monocryl) are synthetic monofilament absorbable sutures, whereas polyglactin (Vicryl) is synthetic braided absorbable.
