domain: 2.7 SURGICAL TUBES, CATHETERS, SUTURES, IMAGING & INSTRUMENTS (13 STATIONS)
stem: After inserting the sterile tube shown into a sedated post-operative patient in the intensive care unit, no fluid can be aspirated for bedside pH testing. Which investigation is definitively required before commencing enteral feeding through this tube?
options: Injecting 20 mL of air while listening over the left hypochondrium
Submerging the proximal funnel in water to check for air bubbles
Advancing the tube 10 cm further and taping it to the forehead
Obtaining a chest/upper abdominal X-ray showing the tip below the diaphragm
Waiting 2 hours and measuring gastric residual volume alone
optionRationales: Incorrect: Air insufflation auscultation ('whoosh test') is unreliable and must never be used to authorise enteral feeding when aspirate pH is unavailable.
Incorrect: Underwater bubble observation is an outdated, unreliable check that risks missing bronchial placement.
Incorrect: Blindly advancing an unconfirmed tube risks coiling or deeper bronchial/parenchymal perforation.

Correct: The packaged device is a Ryles (nasogastric) tube; when gastric aspirate cannot be obtained (or pH > 5.5), a chest/upper abdominal radiograph confirming the radiopaque tip and steel spheres safely below the diaphragm in the stomach is mandatory before feeding.
Incorrect: Waiting without confirming tip position delays care and fails to exclude pulmonary or oesophageal misplacement.
clinicalPearl: If bedside aspirate is unobtainable or pH > 5.5 (e.g., on PPI therapy), confirm Ryles tube position radiographically (tip bisecting the carina, below the left hemidiaphragm, curving into the stomach) before starting feeds.

guideCitation.guideTitle: NG Tube, IC Tube & Urinary Catheter Surgery OSCE Guide
guideCitation.keyPoint: When NG aspirate pH testing is inconclusive or unobtainable, radiographic confirmation (X-ray) is required to verify gastric placement before feeding.

sourceStation.title: Ryles / Nasogastric Tube — Uses & Position Checks
sourceStation.originalPrompt:

stem: A 62-year-old man with Type 2 diabetes mellitus and stage 3 chronic kidney disease is scheduled for the intravenous contrast-enhanced imaging study shown. Alongside checking baseline eGFR and contrast allergies, which oral medication must specifically be identified and temporarily withheld around the procedure?
options: Gliclazide
Atorvastatin
Metformin
Amlodipine
Aspirin
optionRationales: Incorrect: Gliclazide is a sulphonylurea that does not cause contrast-associated lactic acidosis.
Incorrect: Statins do not interact with iodinated contrast to precipitate metabolic acidosis.

Correct: This is a contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) scan; in patients with renal impairment receiving IV iodinated contrast, metformin must be identified and temporarily withheld (typically for 48 hours until renal function is rechecked stable) to prevent metformin-associated lactic acidosis.
Incorrect: Calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine are continued normally around contrast CT imaging.
Incorrect: Low-dose aspirin does not precipitate contrast-induced nephropathy or lactic acidosis.
clinicalPearl: Always ask about Metformin alongside renal disease, contrast/iodine allergy, and pregnancy/LMP before a contrast-enhanced CT; hold metformin if eGFR is reduced and recheck creatinine before restarting.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Preoperative/pre-contrast drug review specifically requires withholding metformin in patients at risk of renal impairment or acute kidney injury.

stem: During closure of a midline laparotomy incision, the scrub nurse passes the surgeon the instrument shown. Which tissue is this instrument specifically designed to grasp securely with minimal crush injury?
options: Tough skin edges and fascial aponeurosis
Delicate small intestinal wall during anastomosis
Exposed median or sciatic nerve trunk
Mesenteric arterial branches before ligation
Visceral pleural surface of the lung
optionRationales: Correct: The instrument shown is a pair of toothed dissecting forceps (1x2 teeth), designed to grip tough structures like skin, fascia, and aponeurosis firmly during suturing without slipping or crushing broader tissue planes.
Incorrect: Toothed forceps perforate and lacerate fragile bowel wall; non-toothed or DeBakey/Babcock forceps are used on intestine.
Incorrect: Grasping nerve trunks with sharp teeth causes iatrogenic neuropraxia or axonotmesis.
Incorrect: Sharp teeth can puncture mesenteric vessels and cause troublesome bleeding; atraumatic vascular forceps (DeBakey) are used instead.
Incorrect: Puncturing visceral pleura with toothed forceps risks air leaks and parenchymal bleeding.
clinicalPearl: Use toothed dissecting forceps strictly on tough tissues (skin, fascia, rectus sheath, aponeurosis); switch to non-toothed or DeBakey forceps for bowel, vessels, peritoneum, and nerves.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Toothed dissecting forceps are included in wound toilet, suturing, herniotomy, and laparotomy packs specifically to hold tough skin and fascial edges firmly during closure.

stem: A 24-year-old man falls onto his outstretched, pronated forearm during a rugby tackle. Forearm and elbow radiographs demonstrate a fracture of the proximal third of the ulna shaft accompanied by anterior dislocation of the radial head. Which eponymous forearm injury is present?
options: Galeazzi fracture-dislocation
Volar Barton's fracture-dislocation
Smith's reversed Colles' fracture
Colles' distal radial fracture
Monteggia fracture-dislocation
optionRationales: Incorrect: A Galeazzi fracture involves the distal radius shaft with dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ) rather than the proximal ulna and radial head.
Incorrect: Barton's fracture is an intra-articular fracture-subluxation of the distal radial rim involving the radiocarpal joint.
Incorrect: Smith's fracture is an extra-articular distal radial fracture within 2.5 cm of the wrist joint with volar displacement.
Incorrect: Colles' fracture is an extra-articular distal radial fracture with dorsal displacement and no proximal radioulnar dislocation.

Correct: Remember 'MUGR' (Monteggia = Ulna proximal fracture + radial head dislocation; Galeazzi = Radius distal fracture + DRUJ dislocation); proximal ulna fracture with radial head dislocation is a Monteggia fracture-dislocation.
clinicalPearl: Always radiograph both joints above and below a single forearm bone fracture using the 'MUGR' mnemonic: Monteggia = proximal Ulna + radial head dislocation; Galeazzi = distal Radius + DRUJ dislocation.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Monteggia fracture-dislocation is an ulnar fracture with radial head dislocation (proximal), whereas Galeazzi is a radial fracture with distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ) dislocation (distal).

domain: 2.7 SURGICAL TUBES, CATHETERS, SUTURES, IMAGING & INSTRUMENTS (13 STATIONS)
stem: A surgical trainee sets up the incision and drainage (I&D) trolley for a fluctuant perianal abscess and is handed a No. 3 Bard-Parker (BP) scalpel handle. Which blade mechanically fits this handle and is specifically designed for making a small, precise stab puncture incision?
options: No. 11 pointed straight blade
No. 20 curved belly blade
No. 22 large curved blade
No. 23 broad curved blade
No. 24 large curved blade
optionRationales: Correct: Blades prefixed with '1' (#10, #11, #12, #15) fit No. 3 and No. 7 BP handles; the pointed triangular #11 blade is specifically designed for small, deep stab/puncture incisions (such as abscess drainage or chest tube skin incisions).
Incorrect: Blades with numeric prefix '2' (20, 21, 22, 23, 24) have a wider slot that fits only the No. 4 BP handle, not the No. 3 handle.
Incorrect: The No. 22 blade is a large curved blade compatible exclusively with a No. 4 BP handle for major skin incisions.
Incorrect: The No. 23 blade requires a No. 4 BP handle (as used in wound toilet/laparotomy packets) rather than a No. 3 handle.
Incorrect: The No. 24 blade fits only the No. 4 BP handle and is unsuitable for delicate stab incisions.
clinicalPearl: Scalpel compatibility rule: Blades starting with '1' (#10, #11, #12, #15) fit No. 3/No. 7 BP handles (#11 for stab punctures, #15 for short shallow incisions); blades starting with '2' (#20–#24) fit No. 4 BP handles.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Blades with numeric prefix '1' (10, 11, 12, 15) fit #3/#7 handles (#11 for tiny deep stab incisions), whereas blades with prefix '2' (20–24) fit #4 handles.

domain: 2.7 SURGICAL TUBES, CATHETERS, SUTURES, IMAGING & INSTRUMENTS (13 STATIONS)
stem: During an open appendicectomy, the surgeon needs to grasp and elevate the inflamed appendix gently without crushing or tearing its friable wall. Which ring-handled instrument from the appendicectomy packet has atraumatic, non-toothed fenestrated jaws designed specifically for tubular viscera?
options: Allis tissue forceps
Kocher's artery forceps
Babcock's forceps
Backhaus towel clip
Curved mosquito haemostat
optionRationales: Incorrect: Allis forceps have sharp inward-pointing teeth intended for grasping tough fascia or rectus sheath and will traumatise delicate bowel or tubular walls.
Incorrect: Kocher's forceps have heavy transverse serrations and a sharp 1x2 interlocking tooth at the tip, causing severe crush injury if applied to bowel or appendix.
Correct: Babcock's forceps feature smooth, non-toothed, fenestrated loop jaws that cradle delicate tubular structures (appendix, ureter, fallopian tube, intestine) atraumatically.
Incorrect: Backhaus towel clips have sharp piercing prongs used exclusively to secure surgical drapes.
Incorrect: Curved mosquito forceps are fine crushing haemostats meant for clamping small bleeding vessels prior to ligation or diathermy.
clinicalPearl: Know the grasping hierarchy: Babcock's (atraumatic, non-toothed loop) for appendix, ureter, and fallopian tube; Allis (sharp teeth) for tough fascia/rectus sheath; Kocher's (toothed heavy clamp) for tough fibrous pedicles.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Babcock's forceps lack sharp teeth and are specifically designed to grasp delicate tubular structures (appendix, fallopian tube, ureter) atraumatically.

domain: 2.3 TRAUMA, SHOCK, BURNS, NEUROTRAUMA & CRITICAL CARE (15 STATIONS)
topic: Chest Drain Massive Haemothorax & Underwater Seal Rules
stem: A 36-year-old man with penetrating right chest trauma has a 32 Fr intercostal chest drain connected to an underwater seal bottle kept below chest level. Immediately upon connection, 1,600 mL of frank blood drains rapidly into the collection chamber while the patient remains hypotensive. What is the most appropriate next definitive surgical step?
options: Clamp the chest tube immediately to tamponade intrathoracic bleeding
Proceed immediately to urgent exploratory surgical thoracotomy
Elevate the underwater seal bottle to chest height to slow drainage
Insert a second 28 Fr chest drain into the 2nd intercostal space
Observe hourly output for 4 hours while giving oral tranexamic acid
optionRationales: Incorrect: Clamping an active chest drain risks tension physiology (haemopneumothorax) and fatal cardiovascular collapse without arresting major vessel bleeding.

Correct: An immediate drainage volume of >= 1,500 mL of blood upon ICD insertion (or ongoing loss > 200 mL/hr) defines massive haemothorax and is an absolute indication for urgent surgical thoracotomy alongside vigorous blood resuscitation.
Incorrect: Elevating the underwater seal bottle above chest level causes retrograde syphoning of fluid/air back into the pleural cavity and must never be done.
Incorrect: Adding a second chest drain does not control an injured internal mammary, intercostal, or pulmonary hilar vessel requiring direct surgical repair.
Incorrect: Conservative observation in a hypotensive patient with 1,600 mL immediate intrathoracic blood loss is fatal; immediate operative control is mandatory.
clinicalPearl: Daily chest drain checks cover patient state, tube function (bubbling, fluid level, respiratory swinging/tidaling), and apparatus (underwater seal intact, bottle strictly below chest level); immediate blood drainage >= 1,500 mL mandates urgent thoracotomy.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Immediate drainage of 1,500 mL of blood upon intercostal chest tube insertion is a classic trauma indication for urgent thoracotomy.

domain: 2.7 SURGICAL TUBES, CATHETERS, SUTURES, IMAGING & INSTRUMENTS (13 STATIONS)
topic: Three-Way Foley Catheter & Continuous Bladder Irrigation
stem: A 70-year-old man develops brisk gross haematuria with blood clots causing painful bladder distension immediately after transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP). Which catheter type and calibre is specifically indicated to establish continuous bladder irrigation (CBI) and prevent recurrent clot obstruction?
options: 12 Fr standard two-way latex Foley catheter
14 Fr straight Nelaton/Robinson intermittent catheter
External penile condom sheath catheter
22 Fr three-way Foley urinary catheter
8 Fr paediatric feeding tube used transurethrally
optionRationales: Incorrect: A narrow 12 Fr two-way Foley catheter lacks a dedicated irrigation inflow channel and rapidly blocks with prostatic blood clots.
Incorrect: A straight Robinson catheter is designed only for single in-and-out drainage and cannot provide indwelling continuous irrigation.
Incorrect: An external condom catheter collects involuntary urinary incontinence externally and does not drain clot-obstructed intravesical retention.

Correct: A large-bore three-way Foley catheter (typically 22 Fr) provides separate channels for balloon inflation, continuous sterile saline irrigation inflow, and wide-lumen outflow to prevent clot retention (while monitoring closely for TURP syndrome: fluid overload and dilutional hyponatraemia).
Incorrect: An 8 Fr paediatric feeding tube is far too narrow for adult post-TURP haematuria and lacks both a retention balloon and irrigation lumen.
clinicalPearl: Use a 22 Fr 3-way Foley catheter for continuous bladder irrigation in gross haematuria/post-TURP bleeding (vs 14–16 Fr 2-way for routine retention); note silicone catheters last up to 3 months vs 1 month for latex, and monitor for TURP syndrome (fluid overload + hyponatraemia).

guideCitation.guideTitle: NG Tube, IC Tube & Urinary Catheter Surgery OSCE Guide
guideCitation.keyPoint: A three-way Foley catheter is an indwelling urethral catheter (typically 22 Fr) inserted specifically for continuous bladder irrigation (CBI) to prevent clot obstruction during bleeding.

domain: 2.5 VASCULAR, DIABETIC FOOT & SOFT-TISSUE INFECTIONS (12 STATIONS)
topic: Digital Ring Block & End-Arterial Vasoconstrictor Contraindication
stem: A 29-year-old carpenter requires wound exploration and nail-bed repair for a deep laceration of his right index finger under a digital ring block at the web space. Which local anaesthetic preparation and maximum dose limit apply safely to prevent digital ischaemia and systemic toxicity?
options: 2% lignocaine with 1:200,000 adrenaline; maximum dose 7 mg/kg
1% lignocaine with 1:80,000 adrenaline; maximum dose 5 mg/kg
0.5% bupivacaine with adrenaline; maximum dose 7 mg/kg
5% bupivacaine hyperbaric spinal solution; maximum dose 3 mg/kg
Plain 1% or 2% lignocaine without adrenaline; maximum dose 3 mg/kg
optionRationales: Incorrect: Although adrenaline raises the safe systemic maximum dose of lignocaine to 7 mg/kg by slowing absorption, adrenaline is strictly avoided in end-arterial sites (digits, tip of nose, earlobe, tip of penis) due to vasospastic ischaemia.
Incorrect: Concentrated 1:80,000 adrenaline injected around digital vessels risks profound arteriolar vasospasm and digital gangrene.
Incorrect: Adrenaline-containing local anaesthetic must not be injected into digital web spaces, and bupivacaine's maximum dose is 2 mg/kg (not 7 mg/kg).
Incorrect: 5% hyperbaric bupivacaine is formulated strictly for intrathecal spinal anaesthesia rather than peripheral ring block.

Correct: Traditional surgical teaching contraindicates adrenaline in end-arterial territories (digits, nose tip, earlobe, tip of penis); perform a web-space ring block using a 25G needle with 2 mL of plain lignocaine (maximum systemic dose 3 mg/kg without adrenaline).
clinicalPearl: Remember the lignocaine dose ceiling and end-arterial rule: max 3 mg/kg plain vs 7 mg/kg with adrenaline (bupivacaine max 2 mg/kg); avoid adrenaline in digits, tip of nose, earlobe, and penis, and remember earliest local anaesthetic toxicity is perioral tingling/agitation.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Use plain lignocaine without adrenaline (max 3 mg/kg; 25G needle, 2 mL at web space) for digital ring blocks, avoiding adrenaline in end-arterial sites (digits, nose tip, earlobe, penis tip).
